props.title: Race with the Devil
props.initialSlug: Two couples battle Satan worshippers in motor home chase

sections.content: Race with the Devil perfectly captures the paranoid zeitgeist of 1970s American horror, blending satanic panic with high-octane car chases. Like Duel (1971) and Vanishing Point (1971), it transforms the American road into a nightmare landscape. The film's genius lies in combining two popular 1970s subgenres - occult horror and car chase action - creating a unique hybrid that influenced later films like The Car (1977) and The Wraith (1986).

sections.content: The film's influence on road horror can't be overstated. Director Jack Starrett brings documentary-style realism to the occult scenes, while the vehicular stunts rival anything in Smokey and the Bandit (1977). Peter Fonda and Warren Oates deliver perfectly paranoid performances that echo the post-Watergate era's distrust of rural America. The film's "trust no one" message predates similar themes in The Wicker Man (1973) and Rosemary's Baby (1968).

The technical achievements deserve special mention. The film's climactic RV chase scenes were revolutionary for their time, shot with multiple cameras at real speed. This approach influenced later horror-on-wheels films like The Hills Have Eyes (1977) and Mad Max (1979). The stunt work, coordinated by legendary Paul Nuckles, set new standards for vehicle-based action sequences. SUBHEAD: Rural Horror and Social Commentary

sections.content: Race with the Devil taps into deeper American anxieties about the rural-urban divide. Like Deliverance (1972) and The Texas Chain Saw Massacre (1974), it presents the countryside as a place of hidden menace. The film's satanic cult represents fears of secret societies operating beneath America's surface, a theme that would later appear in films like Brotherhood of Satan (1971) and The Devil's Rain (1975).
